from:
## Learn One, Read Many

Say this **word**: cat.

Now keep the ending and swap the front. Hat. Bat. Mat. Sat. Rat. Pat.

You just read six new words. You did not learn six new words. You learned one **chunk**, and then you swapped the **start**.

That is a word **family**. All the words end with the same **letters** and the same **sound**.

Here is another one. Hop. Mop. Top. Pop. Same ending, new front each time.

Some fronts have two letters that you say fast together. That is a **blend**. Stop. Chop. Shop. Those are in the same family too.

When words end the same way, they **rhyme**. So a family is a group of words that rhyme.

Every family has a **vowel** in it. The vowels are a, e, i, o and u. The vowel sits in the middle and gives the chunk its sound.

Word families are a **pattern**. Once you spot the pattern, reading gets faster, because you stop sounding out every letter.

But here is something true and a bit annoying. Not every word that rhymes looks the same. Say some and hum. They rhyme. They do not match at all. English does that sometimes.

So use your eyes and your ears. Look for the chunk. Then listen to check.
to:
## Learn One, Read Many

Read this **word** with support: cat. Match each letter to its sound and blend. Now try hat, bat, mat, sat, rat and pat.

The ending **chunk** at stays the same. The **start** changes. These words belong to a spelling **family**: they share ending **letters** and ending **sounds**.

Try hop, mop, top and pop. Their shared ending is op.

In stop, st is a consonant **blend**: you hear /s/ and /t/. In flat, you hear /f/ and /l/. In shop and chop, sh and ch are different: each pair spells one consonant sound. That pair is called a digraph. Shop, chop and stop share the op ending.

Words **rhyme** when their ending sounds match from the vowel onward, as in cat and hat. The **vowel** letters a, e, i, o and u can spell vowel sounds; y sometimes does too. In cat, a is in the middle, but vowel letters are not always in the middle of a written word.

A spelling **pattern** is useful, but check the whole word. Some and hum rhyme in the pronunciation used here even though their endings are spelled differently. Pronunciation can vary across accents.

Look at the letters, use the sound patterns you have learned and blend. Pictures help explain meanings; they do not replace reading the word. Your teacher can provide spoken models or other communication supports.

from: The bit at the front of a word.

from: A group of words that end the same way.

from: Words that end with the same sound.
to: Matching ending sounds from the vowel onward, as in cat and hat.

from: One of these five: a, e, i, o, u.
to: A vowel sound, or a letter that represents one; a, e, i, o, u and sometimes y.

from: Two letters said fast together, like st.
to: Two or more consonant sounds together, each still heard, as in st in stop.

from: Something that happens again and again.
to: A repeated arrangement, such as a shared spelling ending.

from: Now keep the ending and swap the front. You learned one chunk, and then you swapped the start. Say some and hum. They rhyme. They do not match at all.

from: Words in a family end with the same letters.

from: Learning one chunk lets you read many words.

from: Show me a swap with your own hands.

from: You just read six new words. You did not learn six new words.

from: Point to your eyes, then to your ears. Eyes first: does the end look the same? Ears second: does the end sound the same? Two checks, in that order.
to: Compare the written endings and the modeled sounds. Ask for a spoken model or another phonological support that suits your access needs. Check whether the ending letters and sounds match.

from: Pointing at your eyes and then your ears puts the two checks in order and reminds you that one is not enough on its own.
to: Spelling and sound are related but not identical. Use accessible supports for both checks.

from: Say some and hum. They rhyme. They do not match at all.
to: Say some and hum. They rhyme. Their endings have different spellings.

from: English came from lots of languages. The spellings came along too. So a few words look odd. You learn those by heart.
to: English spelling reflects sound patterns and word history. Learn the parts that follow a pattern and pay special attention to an unexpected part. Ask for help with unfamiliar words.

from: Lots. But a few dozen cover most short words. Learn those and a whole shelf of books opens up.
to: There are many useful spelling families. Learn a few at a time alongside letter-sound patterns and practice reading whole words.

from: Say both words slowly, one after the other. Then say just the ends. It gets easier with practice.
to: Ask your teacher for a clear model and support suited to how you communicate. You can compare written endings with guidance; hearing and speaking tasks may need adaptations.

from: They can. In shop, the s and h make one sound together. In chop, the c and h do the same.
to: Yes. Sh in shop and ch in chop each spell one consonant sound; these are digraphs. St in stop is a blend because /s/ and /t/ are both heard.

from: Words in a family end with the same letters.
to: In these spelling families, words share ending letters and ending sounds.

from: Some fronts are blends, like st or ch.
to: Some starts are blends, like st or fl; ch and sh are digraphs, with two letters spelling one sound.

from: Your partner can read every page out loud
to: Your partner can demonstrate reading each page with appropriate communication support

from: A student picked the ending og and kept making words that were not real.
to: A student chose op and checked both the spelling and meaning of each new word.

from: He tried every letter in order and said each one out loud to his partner. They kept dog, log, fog, jog and hog, and put the rest aside.
to: She chose op, tried different starts and checked meanings with her partner and teacher. They kept hop, mop, top, pop and stop. Stop includes the blend st. They set aside unrecognized combinations until they could check whether they were words.

from: Saying each one out loud to somebody caught the made-up ones fast.
to: The example meets the five-word and blend requirements. Not recognizing a word does not prove it is made up; check with a teacher or suitable dictionary.
